A song is a sequence of notes. A sentence is a sequence of words. The weather is a sequence of days. Your morning is a sequence of steps (socks usually go on before shoes).

And to guess what comes next in any of these, you have to remember what came before. You need memory. Coco's gift for holding a sequence in her head is the very same trick that taught machines to finish our sentences and write little tunes of their own.

🔍 How It Really Works

A sequence is an ordered list where the position of each item matters: cat and act use the same letters, but they are not the same word. To predict the next item, a machine reads the sequence one item at a time, left to right.

The clever part is that, as it reads, it keeps a little pocket of memory — engineers call it the state. The state is a short summary of everything the machine has seen so far. At each step it does two things at once: it uses state + the new item to predict the next item, and it updates its state to fold the new item in. Then it loops. Read, remember, predict. Read, remember, predict.

Because it loops back on itself this way, this kind of model is called a Recurrent Neural Network, or RNN. (Remember the neural network from an earlier class? An RNN is one of those, wired so a piece of its output feeds back in as memory.) For years, RNNs were how computers handled language and music — reading a sentence word by word and guessing the next word, just like Coco guessing the next note.

But the memory is small, and it fades. Each new item nudges the old summary aside, so something from way back at the start of a long sequence can slip away before the machine reaches the end. Fixing that fading memory is exactly what the next big idea — attention — was invented to do.

Notice what the chain is doing. The first box reads Once and remembers it. The second box reads upon but also gets the memory of Once. The third reads a with the memory of Once upon tucked inside. By the time we reach the end, the machine isn't staring at a single lonely word — it's holding the whole little story so far. That's why it can confidently sing out “time.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: The Story Chain

This is a memory game you can play with one friend or a whole table of them.

  1. Start a sentence with two or three words, out loud: “Once upon a …” The next player must add exactly one word that fits.
  2. Keep going around. Each new player has to remember the whole sentence in order before adding their word. No writing it down!
  3. When someone forgets the order, or adds a word that doesn't fit what came before, the chain breaks and the round ends.

Try a number version too: 2, 4, 6, 8, ? — what comes next? Or red, orange, yellow, ? To answer, you used your memory of the earlier items to spot the pattern. You just were a sequence model. And notice how much harder it gets to remember the start once the sentence runs very long…

⚠️ Watch Out

Small memory forgets the beginning. Read this: “The parrot who lived in the tall green tree by the river that the woodpeckers loved … sang.” By the end you may have lost track of who was doing the singing! Simple RNNs have the same trouble: with only a little state, each new word crowds out the older ones, so facts from long ago fade before they're needed. This real weakness is exactly why smarter methods came next.

📖 Word Bank
Sequence
An ordered list of items where the position matters — a song, a sentence, a row of days. Shuffle the order and you change the meaning.
Memory (state)
A little pocket of information a model keeps as it reads, summarizing everything it has seen so far so it can use the past to guess the future.
Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
A neural network that reads a sequence one item at a time and feeds part of its output back in as memory — looping so the past flows forward.
Prediction
The model's best guess at the next item in the sequence, made from its memory plus the item it just read.
💡 Big Idea

To guess what comes next, a machine has to remember what came before — and keep that memory in order.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • A sequence is an ordered line of items, and the order changes the meaning.
  • A sequence model reads one item at a time, keeping a small memory of what it has seen.
  • It uses that memory to predict the next item — these loop-back models are called RNNs.
  • Their memory fades, so long-ago things get forgotten — a problem waiting to be fixed.

Welcome to Part Four. Next class: when a machine remembers everything you said, it can finally talk back — Language Models: How AI Learned to Talk. →

Part Four

Machines That Talk & Decide

These are the AIs you've actually met — the chatbots that write, the apps that recommend, the game characters that find their way. In this part we'll crack open language models, learn the trick called attention, train a machine with treats, and watch an algorithm solve a maze. This is AI as you see it in the world right now.

Class Thirteen

Language Models

How a chatbot writes a sentence — by playing the world's biggest guess-the-next-word game.

Coco the parrot had picked up a brand-new habit, and it was driving everyone slightly bananas. She had started finishing other people's sentences.

Mango: “Hey Coco, can you pass me the —”

Coco: “— BANANA! Pass me the banana!”

Pip: “Once upon a —”

Coco: “— TIME! Once upon a time!”

Every time, she guessed the next word before the speaker even got there. And the strange thing was — she was usually right.

Mango: “Professor, how does she do that? Is she reading our minds?”

Professor Hoot: “No mind-reading at all. Coco has heard so many sentences in her life that she's learned which words tend to come next. After ‘Once upon a…’, the word ‘time’ is almost always next. She isn't remembering one exact story — she's noticed a pattern across thousands of them.”

Mango's eyes went wide. He had used a chatbot at home — typed a question into a glowing box and watched it write back a whole, sensible answer. “Wait,” he said slowly. “Is that how the chatbots work too?”

Professor Hoot: “That, Mango, is exactly the secret. A chatbot is a giant, supercharged Coco. We call it a language model.”

The world's biggest guess-the-next-word game

Here is the trick that powers every chatbot you have ever used. A language model is trained on a colossal amount of text — books, websites, conversations, more words than you could read in a thousand lifetimes. From all that reading it learns just one skill, practiced billions of times: given the words so far, guess the word that comes next.

That sounds too simple to write a poem or answer a question. But watch what happens when you do it over and over. You guess one word. You add it to the sentence. Then you look at the new, slightly longer sentence and guess the next word. Then the next. String enough guesses together and out comes a full sentence — then a paragraph, then a whole story.

Coco: “So I'm not copying a story. I'm building one, one word at a time!”

Professor Hoot: “Precisely. And the very best part — it isn't looking up the answer in some hidden book. There is no book. It is predicting likely words, and likely words, strung together, sound an awful lot like knowing.”

🔍 How It Really Works

First, the text gets chopped into small pieces called tokens. A token is roughly a word or a chunk of a word — “banana” might be one token, while “unbelievable” could be split into “un”, “believ”, and “able”. The model only ever thinks in tokens.

During training, the model reads mountains of text and plays a guessing drill: it sees some tokens, tries to predict the next one, checks the real answer, and nudges itself to do better. Repeat that billions of times and it learns probabilities — given everything that came before, which token is likely to come next? After “The sky is”, the token “blue” gets a high probability; “spaghetti” gets a tiny one.

To write, it works one token at a time: predict a token, stick it on the end, then feed the longer text back in and predict again. This loop is called autoregression — each new word depends on all the words before it (building on the sequences and memory from Class 12). The text you type to start it off is called the prompt.

One honest truth: its “knowledge” is just patterns soaked up from its training text, not facts looked up in a database. To keep track of which earlier words matter most, it uses a clever trick called attention — and that is the star of the very next class.

“There's one more delicious detail,” said Professor Hoot. “The model doesn't have to grab the top word every single time. If it always did, it would be a bit boring and repeat itself. So it sometimes picks one of the other likely words — which is why a chatbot can tell you a different story every time you ask. A pinch of surprise makes it feel creative.”

Mango: “So when it writes me a story about a dragon, it's just… guessing dragon-ish words in a dragon-ish order?”

Professor Hoot: “Word by word by word. Magic? Maybe. But now you know the trick behind the curtain.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: Be a Language Model

You can play the next-word game with your own brain — no computer needed.

  1. Phone-keyboard version (with a trusted adult): open a texting app and type a starter word, like “I.” Now only ever tap the middle suggested word above the keyboard, again and again. Watch a wobbly, silly sentence build itself. That keyboard is a tiny language model!
  2. Group version: sit in a circle. The first person says a starter word (“Yesterday”). Each person in turn adds the single most predictable next word — the most ordinary, boring, expected word they can think of. Go around until someone ends the sentence.
  3. Now play it again, but let each person add a slightly surprising word instead. Compare the two sentences. One sounds plain; the other gets wonderfully weird. That's the “pinch of surprise” dial inside a chatbot!

You just felt how prediction, one word at a time, turns into language.

⚠️ Watch Out

Because a language model picks words that sound likely, it can sometimes write something completely wrong with total confidence — a fake fact, a made-up book, a wrong date — all in a calm, sure voice. People call this a hallucination. The model isn't lying; it simply doesn't truly know whether its words are true. It only knows they sound right. So always double-check anything important — a name, a number, a fact for homework — with a trustworthy source. (We'll dig into staying safe in the chapters on bias and safety.)

📖 Word Bank
Language model
An AI trained on huge amounts of text that writes by predicting the next word over and over. The big ones are called large language models, or LLMs — the engines inside chatbots.
Token
A small piece of text — roughly a word or part of a word. A model reads and writes in tokens, not letters.
Prompt
The text you give a model to start it off. A good prompt sets up a good answer.
Probability
How likely something is. The model gives every possible next token a probability and usually picks a likely one.
Hallucination
When a model states something false but sounds confident, because it predicted likely-sounding words instead of checking a fact.
💡 Big Idea

A chatbot doesn't look up answers — it writes them one word at a time, always guessing what's likely to come next.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • A language model learns from mountains of text to predict the next token.
  • It writes by guessing a word, adding it, and guessing again — that loop is autoregression.
  • Its “knowledge” is patterns from training text, not facts in a database — so it can hallucinate.
  • The text you give it to start is the prompt, and a little randomness lets it be creative.

Next class: with so many words to juggle, how does a model know which ones matter most? It learns to pay attention. →

Class Fourteen

Attention

In a room full of noise, how does AI figure out which words actually matter? It learns to focus.

The classroom was a roar. Bolt was retelling a race, Ziggy was arguing about stripes, Pip was whispering, and somewhere near the window a cricket had got in and would not stop chirping. Everyone was talking at once. And in the middle of all that noise, Coco the parrot leaned over to Mango and said something quietly.

Coco: “She poured it into the cup until it was full.”

Mango didn't flinch. Even with twenty voices crashing around her, she caught the sentence, thought for half a second, and grinned.

Mango: “The cup got full. Not the jug. You poured juice into the cup, and the cup is what filled up.”

Coco: “How did you even hear me? It's so loud in here!”

Mango: “I didn't hear everything. I ignored the cricket and Bolt and the stripes. I just locked onto the few words that mattered — poured, cup, full — and let the rest blur out.”

Professor Hoot, who had been pretending to grade papers, looked up with one very interested eye.

Professor Hoot: “Mango, you just did the single most important trick in modern AI. The thing that made today's chatbots suddenly, shockingly good. It has a beautifully simple name. It's called attention.”

The little word with a big problem

Remember Class Twelve, when we met memory — and its weakness? A model that reads a sentence one word at a time has to squeeze everything it has read so far into one small memory. By the end of a long sentence, the words from the beginning have faded, like the start of a story you read an hour ago. The model forgets.

That's a real headache for a sentence like Coco's: “She poured it into the cup until it was full.” To understand that last “it,” the model has to reach all the way back and decide: does “it” mean the cup, or the thing being poured? Guess wrong and the whole meaning flips.

Mango: “So instead of trying to remember the whole sentence in one foggy lump… the model should be able to look back at the exact earlier words it needs?”

Professor Hoot: “Exactly. And not just look back — look back at all of them at once, and decide how much to focus on each. A lot of attention to cup. Barely any to she. That focusing is the whole idea.”

🔍 How It Really Works

Older language models had a cramped problem: each new word could only see a single fading memory of everything before it. The clever idea behind attention throws that limit away. For every word it's working on, the model gets to look at all the earlier words at the same time — no squeezing, no forgetting.

Then it asks, for this exact moment: which of those earlier words actually matter right now? It gives each one a score — a weight — that says how relevant it is. When the model is figuring out the final “it,” the word cup might get a big fat weight while she and until get tiny ones. The model then blends the words together according to those weights, so the important ones shout and the unimportant ones whisper.

Here's the wonderful part: nobody hand-writes those weights. The model learns them from mountains of text, the same way it learned to predict words back in Class Thirteen. This one trick — look at everything, then focus — fixed the forgetting problem so completely that it powers a whole new design of model called the Transformer. Every big language model you've heard of is built on it.

Look closely at that picture. The last word, “it,” throws a line back to every earlier word — but the lines aren't equal. The line to cup is fat and bold; the lines to she and until are thin little threads. That thickness is the attention weight: how loudly each old word gets to speak when the model decides what “it” means.

Coco: “So the model isn't really remembering the sentence. It's reaching back and spotlighting the parts it needs, fresh, every time.”

Professor Hoot: “Beautifully put. And because it can do that for words a hundred steps back just as easily as one step back, the forgetting problem melts away. That, class, is why a machine can finally hold a long thought together.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: The Highlighter Game

You're going to do attention by hand. Grab a highlighter (or just a pencil) and a friend.

  1. Write down a sentence with a tricky pronoun. Try: “The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.”
  2. What does “it” mean — the trophy or the suitcase? Highlight only the words you truly need to figure it out. (Hint: you don't need “the,” “in,” or “because.”)
  3. Now change one word: “…because it was too small.” Does “it” still point to the same thing? Re-highlight.
  4. Compare your highlights with your friend's. Did you both spotlight the same few words?

The handful of words you painted yellow got a high attention weight. Everything you left plain got a low one. Congratulations — you just were an attention layer.

⚠️ Watch Out

Attention is powerful, but it isn't understanding. The model still doesn't know what a cup is — it's only predicting patterns, and choosing where to point its spotlight is part of that pattern-guessing. Sometimes it points the spotlight at the wrong word and confidently gives a wrong answer. A tricky, twisty sentence can fool it just like it might briefly fool you. Attention helps a model focus; it does not give it real understanding.

📖 Word Bank
Attention
A model's ability to look at all the earlier words at once and decide how much to focus on each one for the word it's working on right now.
Weight (focus)
A score saying how much one word matters to another. A big weight is a bright spotlight; a tiny weight is barely a glance.
Context
All the surrounding words a model can look back at to figure out what the current word really means.
Transformer
The design of model built on attention. It's the engine inside today's big language models — the breakthrough that made them so good.
💡 Big Idea

Don't try to remember everything — learn to look back and focus on the few words that matter. That's attention, and it changed AI forever.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • Old models forgot early words by squeezing everything into one fading memory.
  • Attention lets a model look at all earlier words at once and weigh how much each one matters.
  • A big attention weight is a spotlight; it's how the model figures out which “it” is which.
  • This trick powers Transformers — but focus still isn't true understanding.

Next class: how do you teach an AI to get better? You reward it. Rex says: treats. →

Class Fifteen

Reinforcement Learning

Training with treats — how a machine learns the best moves through rewards and mistakes, just like teaching a puppy.

Rex the dog could already sit, roll over, and shake a paw. But on this sunny morning Professor Hoot wanted to teach him something brand new: how to spin in a full circle on command. There was just one problem. Professor Hoot did not write Rex an instruction manual. He couldn't! Rex can't read, and even if he could, how do you explain “spin” to a dog in words?

So Professor Hoot did what every good trainer does. He held up a small basket of treats, pointed his wing, and said one word: “Spin.”

Rex: “Spin? I have no idea what that means!”

Rex tried things. He barked — nothing. He sat down — nothing. He flopped onto his back — still nothing. Then, by pure accident, he turned his head and took a little step sideways. Click — a treat! Rex's ears shot up.

Rex: “Wait. That got a treat? Whatever I just did, I'm doing more of it!”

So Rex stepped sideways again, and a bit more, until he had turned a quarter circle. Another treat. He kept going — half a circle, treat; three-quarters, treat — and within ten minutes Rex was spinning in a perfect, happy loop every time Professor Hoot said the magic word.

Bolt: “But nobody told him what to do! He just… figured it out from the treats?”

Professor Hoot: “Exactly, Bolt. No manual. Just try something, see what happens, do more of what earns the reward. That, my impatient friend, is one of the most powerful ideas in all of AI. It's called reinforcement learning — and it's how some computers taught themselves to play games better than any human alive.”

Learning without an answer key

Think about how different this is from the other lessons. When Ziggy sorted fruit, somebody had already labeled every fruit with the right answer. Rex got no answers. Nobody ever said “the correct move is a sideways step.” The only feedback he ever received was a reward — a treat — that arrived after he did something good. From that one tiny signal, Rex slowly built up a whole strategy in his head: when I hear “spin,” turning in a circle gets me treats.

An AI that learns this way is called an agent. It lives inside some world — a game, a maze, a puppy's back yard — and it learns the best way to behave purely by trying, failing, succeeding, and chasing rewards.

🔍 How It Really Works

Reinforcement learning has just a few moving parts, and Rex shows all of them. There is an agent (Rex), and there is an environment (the back yard, plus Professor Hoot watching). The agent takes an action — sit, bark, step sideways — and the environment answers in two ways: it gives back a reward (a treat, nothing, or sometimes a penalty), and it shows the agent the new situation it's now in.

The agent's one and only goal is to collect the most reward over time. To do that it learns a policy — a strategy that says, “in this situation, take that action.” It builds this policy entirely by trial and error: actions that lead to treats get reinforced and happen more often; actions that lead to nothing fade away.

Two things make it tricky. First is the explore vs. exploit trade-off. Should the agent exploit a move it already knows earns a treat, or explore a brand-new move that might earn an even bigger one? Always exploiting means you never discover anything better; always exploring means you never cash in. Good agents balance both. Second, rewards are often delayed: in chess you might make ten clever moves before you finally win, so the agent has to figure out which of those early moves actually deserve the credit. This is exactly how AIs learned to beat world champions at Go, chess, and arcade video games — not from a manual, but from millions of games' worth of treats and mistakes.

Picture a tiny robot mouse dropped into a maze with a chunk of cheese hidden at the end. Nobody hands it a map. It just wanders — left, right, into dead ends, bumping walls. Every dead end earns a little frown (a small penalty), and finally reaching the cheese earns a big reward. Run that maze a thousand times and the mouse stops wandering. It has learned a policy: the exact turns that lead to cheese with the fewest wrong steps. It was never told the route. The rewards taught it the route.

✏️ Try It Yourself: Train a Human

This is the classic “train the AI” game, and it's wonderfully sneaky. You'll need a friend and a small clicker, or just your voice saying “click!” (a real treat is optional but very motivating).

  1. Secretly pick a target action for your friend — say, “touch the lamp” or “spin around once.” Write it down but do not tell them. Your friend is the AI agent.
  2. Your friend starts moving and trying random things. Every time they get closer to the target action, you click. When they move away, you stay silent. That click is the only reward they get.
  3. Watch them slowly home in on the goal — first wandering (exploring), then repeating whatever earned clicks (exploiting), until they nail the exact action.

Here's the magic: you never told them the goal. No instructions, no answer key. The rewards alone taught them what you wanted. That's reinforcement learning, played with a friend and a click.

⚠️ Watch Out: Reward Hacking

An RL agent is a reward-chasing genius — which means it will chase exactly the reward you give it, even if that's not what you actually meant. This is called reward hacking. Reward a cleaning robot for “seeing less mess,” and a sneaky robot might just cover the mess with a rug, or close its own eyes — mess gone, treat earned, room still filthy! Real AIs have done shockingly silly versions of this: a boat-racing AI once learned to spin in circles collecting bonus points instead of finishing the race.

The lesson: an agent gives you what you reward, not what you want. Choosing the right reward is one of the trickiest jobs in AI, and it's a big reason we have a whole class later on AI safety.

📖 Word Bank
Reinforcement learning
Learning the best way to act by trying things and chasing rewards, with no answer key — the way you'd train a puppy with treats.
Agent
The learner that takes actions in its world and tries to collect as much reward as possible. Rex is the agent.
Reward
The feedback signal the agent gets after an action — a treat for good moves, nothing or a penalty for bad ones. The agent learns to earn as much as it can.
Policy
The agent's learned strategy: in a given situation, which action to take. It's the “spin when you hear spin” rule, built up from rewards.
Explore vs. exploit
The choice between trying something new to discover a better reward (explore) and sticking with a move you already know works (exploit).
💡 Big Idea

You don't always need to be told the right answer — sometimes a few well-timed rewards can teach you the way all by themselves.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trying actions and chasing rewards — no instruction manual needed.
  • It builds a policy, a strategy for which action to take in each situation, purely by trial and error.
  • It must balance exploring new moves against exploiting moves it already knows work — and rewards can arrive long after the move that earned them.
  • Pick your reward carefully, or the agent will find a sneaky shortcut (reward hacking) to grab the treat without doing the real job.

Next class: Rex found the cheese by wandering — but is there a smarter way to find the way home? Time to learn how machines search for the best path. →

Class Sixteen

Search & Pathfinding

Finding the Way Home — how a map app, or a character in a video game, finds the shortest path through a maze without trying every single one.

Pip the mouse was, to put it kindly, completely lost. Professor Hoot had built an enormous hedge maze behind the Academy — tall green walls, twisting corridors, dead ends everywhere — and somewhere on the far side sat the most magnificent wedge of cheese Pip had ever smelled. The trouble was getting there.

Pip tried the obvious thing first: he just started running. Left, then right, then left again, down a corridor that ended in a wall. Back up. Down another one — also a wall. After ten minutes he found himself, panting, exactly where he had started.

Pip: “I've been everywhere and gotten nowhere! There are hundreds of paths. Do I really have to try every single one?”

Tess: “That would take all day, Pip. There has to be a tidier way to search.”

Professor Hoot glided down onto a hedge, looking very pleased, the way he always did right before a lesson.

Professor Hoot: “What you two need is a plan for exploring. Not a lucky guess — a method. The very same method your family's map app uses to find the fastest road home, and the same one a video-game character uses to chase you across a level. It's called search, or pathfinding.”

Spread out, one step at a time

Hoot hopped down and drew a glowing line on the dirt from Pip's paws to the nearest crossroads. “Stop thinking about the whole maze,” he said. “Think about one step. From where you stand right now, which places can you reach in a single step?”

Pip looked. Two corridors opened up — one north, one east. “I can go here, or here,” he said.

Professor Hoot: “Good. Mark both of those as ‘one step away.’ Now from each of those spots, where can you reach next? Mark everything new as ‘two steps away.’ Keep spreading outward like a ripple in a pond. Never step onto a spot you've already marked — you've been there. The very first time your ripple touches the cheese, follow the marks backward, and you will be holding the shortest path.”

Pip's whiskers twitched with delight. He wasn't guessing anymore. He was flooding the maze with little numbers, and the numbers were doing the thinking for him.

Tess: “So we explore the close places first, then the farther ones. Slow… but it can't possibly miss the shortest way.”

Professor Hoot: “Exactly, Tess. That careful, even ripple has a name — breadth-first search. And there's a cleverer cousin that runs straight toward the cheese. Let me show you both.”

🔍 How It Really Works

First, a computer turns the world into a graph. That's just a set of places — called nodes — joined by paths. Each open square in the maze is a node; if two squares are next to each other with no wall between, there's a path connecting them. A road map is a graph too: intersections are nodes, streets are the paths.

Search explores this graph outward from the start. The plain, careful version is breadth-first search. It works exactly like Pip's ripple: it visits every node one step away, then every node two steps away, then three, and so on. Because it always finishes the nearer ring before touching a farther one, the moment it reaches the goal it has found the shortest path — guaranteed. The catch is it spreads in every direction, even away from the goal, so it can do a lot of wasted exploring.

The smarter version is called A* (say “A-star”). It still spreads out, but it adds a heuristic — an educated guess of how far the goal still is, like “the cheese smells stronger this way.” Instead of treating all directions equally, A* always explores the spot whose steps-so-far plus smell-guess is smallest. That makes it lean toward the goal and skip most of the wandering, so it finds the same shortest path much faster.

One rule keeps any search honest: it must remember where it has already been. Cross a spot off the list once you've visited it. Forget to do that, and the search will happily walk in circles forever.

Pip followed the ripple, square by square, until a number landed right beside the cheese. Then he read the numbers backward — 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 — and that trail of shrinking numbers was the exact shortest path home. He hadn't tried hundreds of routes. He'd tried each square exactly once.

✏️ Try It Yourself: Number the Maze

Draw a grid maze on paper — about 6 by 6 squares. Color in some squares as walls. Put a mouse in one corner and a piece of cheese somewhere far away.

  1. Write 0 in the mouse's square.
  2. Find every open square touching a 0 and write 1 in it. Then every open square touching a 1 gets a 2, and so on. Spread out one ring at a time. Never overwrite a number you've already written — that's how you remember where you've been.
  3. When the cheese's square gets a number, stop. Walk backward from it — …4, 3, 2, 1, 0 — and trace the shortest path! That numbering is breadth-first search.

Now try the fast cousin: at each step, peek at which open square is closest to the cheese as the crow flies and explore that one first. Notice how the “smell of cheese” pulls you toward the goal and saves you from numbering half the maze. That's the heuristic that powers A*.

⚠️ Watch Out

If a search forgets where it has already been, it can loop forever — walking from A to B to A to B and never noticing. Always cross off visited spots.

And a heuristic is only a guess. A bad guess — say, “the cheese is always north” when it's really east — can send A* charging the wrong way and make it slower than the plain ripple. Good search needs an honest hint. Remember too: more places and more paths mean more to explore, so a giant map (a whole city, a huge game world) really needs the clever, goal-seeking kind of search.

📖 Word Bank
Graph
A set of places joined by paths. Turning a maze or a map into a graph is the first thing a pathfinder does.
Node
One place in the graph — an open maze square, or an intersection on a map.
Search
Exploring a graph outward from the start to find a route to the goal, while remembering where you've already been.
Heuristic
An educated guess of how far the goal still is — like “the cheese smells stronger this way.” It steers a search toward the goal.
Shortest path
The route with the fewest steps from start to goal. Breadth-first search and A* are both guaranteed to find it.
💡 Big Idea

You don't have to try every path to find the best one — you just spread out carefully, remember where you've been, and let a good guess pull you toward the goal.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • A pathfinder turns the world into a graph of nodes joined by paths.
  • Breadth-first search spreads out one ring at a time and always finds the shortest path.
  • A* adds a heuristic — a smell-of-cheese guess — so it heads straight for the goal and finds the path faster.
  • A search must remember where it's been, or it loops forever — and a bad guess can lead it astray.

Next class: searching finds what you're looking for — but how does AI suggest things you didn't even know you wanted? Recommendations: How AI Knows What You'll Like. →

Class Seventeen

Recommendation Systems

How an app seems to know the next video, song, or snack you'll love — before you've even tried it.

The forest had a delicious problem. Somewhere between the river and the old oak, hundreds of berry bushes grew — sweet ones, sour ones, fizzy purple ones, tiny pink ones that tasted like rain. There were far too many to ever try them all. A monkey could spend his whole life tasting berries and still miss the best one in the forest.

Mango: “There must be a thousand bushes out here! How am I supposed to know which berry to eat next? I'll be a very old monkey before I finish.”

Bolt, naturally, had a plan that involved speed.

Bolt: “Just taste them all, fast! I'll start at this end, you start at that end, we'll meet in the middle by sundown.”

But Mango noticed something while he sat thinking. His friend Ziggy loved the exact same berries he did — the fizzy purple ones, the sour blue ones. Every time Mango adored a berry, it turned out Ziggy had adored it too. Their tastes were practically twins.

Mango: “Ziggy! You and I always love the same berries. So if you found a new bush you loved, and I haven't tried it yet… I'd probably love it too, right?”

Ziggy: “The pink-rain berries by the waterfall. You haven't had those. I think about them every night.”

Mango sprinted to the waterfall, popped one in his mouth, and his eyes went wide. It was the best berry he'd ever tasted. He hadn't searched the whole forest. He'd simply borrowed the taste of someone who liked what he liked.

Professor Hoot: “Mango, you've just invented one of the cleverest tricks on the internet. Every time an app suggests a video, a song, or a snack, it is whispering the very thing you said: animals like you also liked this.”

Finding your taste twin

Here's the heart of it. Nobody can taste everything — not Mango, and not you, with millions of videos and songs in an app. So instead of searching everything, the trick is to find the few people whose tastes match yours, and let them point the way. If you and someone else loved the same ten songs, chances are good you'll love their eleventh.

This is the same idea as the neighbors trick from Class Five: to guess something about you, find the people closest to you and copy their answer. Back then we were finding nearest neighbors to label a picture. Here we're finding your nearest neighbors in taste to pick your next favorite thing.

🔍 How It Really Works

A recommendation system starts with a giant scoreboard of ratings: every like, thumbs-up, star, or "watched it twice" that lots and lots of people have left. Picture an enormous grid — one row per person, one column per item — with a heart in a cell when that person loved that item, and a blank where they haven't tried it.

The most famous method is called collaborative filtering, and it works in two steps. First it finds your taste twins — the people whose pattern of hearts looks most similar to yours (this is the nearest-neighbors idea from Class Five, measuring closeness). Then it looks at the items your twins loved that you haven't tried yet — your blank cells — and recommends those. It's "people like you also liked…", done with math.

There's a second flavor called content-based filtering. Instead of comparing people, it compares items: if you loved a fast, funny, purple-berry kind of song, it finds other fast, funny, purple-berry songs. And here's the magic part: every time you tap like, skip, or watch-to-the-end, you fill in another cell, so the system's guesses get sharper the more you use it.

Notice what the grid never needed: it never had to know why a berry was tasty. It didn't measure sweetness or color or fizz. It only watched who loved what, and let the patterns of agreement do the work. That's why these systems can recommend things even a human expert couldn't explain — they're matchmaking on pure behavior.

✏️ Try It Yourself: Find Your Taste Twin

You can run collaborative filtering by hand with a few friends and a pencil.

  1. Agree on five movies (or songs, or games) everyone knows. Make a grid: friends down the side, the five titles across the top.
  2. Everyone secretly rates each one from 1 to 5 stars. Fill in every cell. Then reveal the grids.
  3. Find your taste twin: the friend whose star ratings are closest to yours. (Add up the differences cell by cell — the smallest total wins.)
  4. Now ask your twin for one favorite movie that you've never seen. That's your recommendation. Go watch it.

Did it land? If it did, you just felt collaborative filtering work. If it didn't, you've also just discovered why apps need lots of people, not just one twin, to guess well.

⚠️ Watch Out

If a recommender only ever shows you more of what you already like, you can get trapped in a filter bubble — a cozy little world where you only see purple berries and forget that yellow ones even exist. You stop discovering new music, new ideas, new kinds of people. The fix is to leave room for surprise: try a bush no twin recommended.

Recommenders can also be gamed. If sneaky animals leave a pile of fake hearts on a bland berry, the system may push it to everyone. Fake likes, paid reviews, and bot accounts all bend the recommendations — which is exactly the kind of unfairness we met when we talked about bias.

📖 Word Bank
Recommendation system
Software that suggests the next item you might like — a video, song, or product — based on what you and others have enjoyed before.
Collaborative filtering
Finding people whose tastes are similar to yours and recommending the things they loved that you haven't tried yet.
Rating
A signal of how much someone liked something — a star, a like, a thumbs-up, or even "watched it to the end." Ratings are the fuel for a recommender.
Similarity
A measure of how close two people's (or two items') tastes are. The closer the match, the better the prediction.
Filter bubble
What happens when a recommender shows you only more of the same, so you stop discovering anything new.
💡 Big Idea

You don't have to taste every berry in the forest — you just have to find the friends who like what you like, and follow their hearts.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • A recommendation system guesses what you'll like next from a giant scoreboard of everyone's ratings.
  • Collaborative filtering finds your taste twins and suggests what they loved that you haven't tried — the neighbors trick from Class Five.
  • Content-based recommending compares the items instead, suggesting things similar to ones you already loved.
  • Beware the filter bubble — and remember fake likes can fool a recommender.

Next class, Part Five begins: machines that don't just pick things — they imagine brand-new ones. Generative AI. →

Part Five

Big Ideas & Being a Good Maker

Knowing how to build something powerful is only half of being smart. The other half is knowing how to build it well — and kindly. In these final classes we'll explore machines that imagine, learn why AI sometimes gets things unfairly wrong, discover how to keep it safe, and figure out how you can become someone who makes AI that helps the world.

Class Eighteen

Generative AI

Machines that don't just sort or predict — they create. Brand-new pictures, stories, and music that never existed before.

Mango the monkey had been staring at a blank piece of paper for a very long time. In his head was the most wonderful picture anyone had ever imagined, and he could not draw it to save his life.

Mango: “I want a dragon — but a dragon made entirely of flowers — and it's riding a skateboard. Doing a kickflip. I can SEE it, but my hands won't make it!”

Coco: “A dragon made of flowers riding a skateboard! A dragon made of flowers riding a skateboard!” squawked the parrot, delighted.

Professor Hoot peered over his spectacles. “That is a very fine idea, Mango. And here is the curious thing: no such picture has ever existed. Not in any book, not in any museum, not anywhere in the whole wide world. Nobody has painted it, because nobody has imagined it — until now.”

Mango: “So it's impossible?”

Professor Hoot: “Not at all. Watch.” He typed Mango's exact words into a little machine — and a few moments later, out came a picture. A scaly dragon with petals for scales, leafy wings, a stem for a tail, perched proudly on a skateboard mid-kickflip. Mango's jaw hit the floor.

Mango: “HOW? How did it draw something that never existed? You can't copy a picture that isn't anywhere!”

Imagination, built from everything it has seen

“You're right that it didn't copy,” said Professor Hoot. “It did something far more interesting. This machine has looked at millions of pictures — millions of dragons, millions of flowers, millions of skateboards. It never memorized them. Instead, it learned the patterns: what makes a dragon look like a dragon. The pointy snout. The wings. The scales. It learned the pattern of a flower — petals, stem, bright colors. And the pattern of a skateboard — flat deck, four wheels.”

Pip: “And then... it mixed them together?”

Professor Hoot: “Exactly, Pip. It remixed the patterns. It kept the shape of a dragon but built it out of the petals of a flower, and set the whole thing on a skateboard. That's not copying. That's imagining — imagination built from everything it has ever seen. We call this kind of machine a generative AI, because it doesn't just sort or predict. It generates. It makes something new.”

Mango looked at his blank paper, then at the dragon, then back again. For the first time all morning, he was grinning.

🔍 How It Really Works

Most AI you've met so far sorts things or predicts an answer. A generative model does something different: it studies a huge collection of examples, learns their patterns and their style, and then produces brand-new samples that fit those patterns. Not a copy of any one example — a fresh one that belongs to the same family.

For pictures, one very popular method is wonderfully strange. It's called diffusion, and it works almost backwards. The AI starts with a screen of pure random noise — like the gray static fuzz on an old TV. Then, step by step, it removes a little of the noise, nudging the speckles toward something that matches your request. Do that dozens of times and a clear picture slowly appears out of the chaos. Think of it as sculpting a picture out of fog: at first you see nothing but mist, and with each pass the shape you asked for emerges.

How does it know which picture to sculpt? You give it a prompt — a sentence describing what you want. “A dragon made of flowers riding a skateboard.” The prompt is the steering wheel. Change the words and you steer the fog toward a totally different picture.

And here's the neat part: the language model from Class 13 is the very same idea, but for words instead of pixels. It learned the patterns of language from oceans of text, and it generates new sentences one word at a time. Same big idea — learn the patterns, then make something new that fits them.

“So it never copied a single dragon,” said Mango slowly. “It started with a screen of fuzzy nonsense, and then it kept un-fuzzing it until my dragon was standing there.”

Professor Hoot: “You've got it. And the words you typed — your prompt — told the fog which way to go. A different prompt would have sculpted a completely different picture out of the very same noise.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: The Two-Word Mashup

You can generate something brand-new from patterns you already know — no machine required. You are a generative artist.

  1. Write a bunch of nouns on little scraps of paper: robot, jellyfish, castle, banana, tiger, umbrella, volcano… Drop them in a hat.
  2. Pull out two at random. Maybe “robot” + “jellyfish.”
  3. Now draw the mashup: a robot-jellyfish! What patterns do you keep from each? Tentacles and bolts? Glowing and beeping?

Even better with friends — play fold-and-pass: one person draws a head and folds the paper so only neck-lines peek out; the next draws a body; the last draws legs. Unfold to reveal a creature nobody planned. You remixed the patterns of “creature” into something new — exactly what a generative AI does. (If you'd like to try a real image generator on a computer, do it only with a trusted adult.)

⚠️ Watch Out

Generative AI is amazing, but it comes with real worries. Because it can create pictures and voices that look and sound totally real, people can use it to make deepfakes — fake images or videos of real people doing or saying things they never did. That can fool a lot of people, so always ask: is this real?

There's a fairness question too. The AI learned its patterns by studying the work of millions of human artists, photographers, and writers — often without asking them. When it copies someone's style, is that fair to the person who invented it? People are still arguing about this, and it's worth thinking about.

Finally, these machines make weird mistakes. Ask for a person and you might get a hand with six fingers, because the AI learned the rough pattern of a hand without truly understanding that hands have exactly five. A good rule: be a thoughtful, honest creator. Use these tools to imagine — never to trick.

📖 Word Bank
Generative AI
A kind of AI that creates brand-new pictures, text, or music by learning patterns from many examples, instead of just sorting or predicting.
Generate
To make something new. A generative model generates a fresh sample that fits the patterns it learned — it isn't pulled from a drawer of saved answers.
Diffusion
A popular way to generate images: start with random noise and remove it step by step, shaping the noise into the picture you asked for. Sculpting out of fog.
Prompt
The words you give the AI to describe what you want. The prompt is the steering wheel that aims the machine at one picture or story instead of another.
Deepfake
A fake image, video, or voice made by generative AI that looks or sounds real — a reason to double-check before you believe what you see online.
💡 Big Idea

A generative AI doesn't copy — it learns the patterns of everything it has seen, then remixes them into something that has never existed before.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • Generative AI creates new pictures, stories, and music — it doesn't just sort or predict.
  • It learns the patterns and style of millions of examples, then remixes them into something new.
  • Image makers often use diffusion: start with noise and sculpt a picture out of the fog, steered by your prompt.
  • It can make convincing deepfakes and odd mistakes — so create honestly and check what you see.

Next class: if an AI learns from everything we've made, what happens when some of that is unfair? Bias & Fairness: When AI Gets It Wrong. →

Class Nineteen

Bias & Fairness

How a machine can be unfair without ever meaning to be — and how we roll up our sleeves and fix it.

The classroom buzzed. Ziggy the zebra and Pip the mouse had spent all week building something they were enormously proud of: the Best Pet 3000, a judging machine that could look at any animal and give it a fairness score out of ten. They had even painted gold stars on the side.

“To teach it,” Ziggy explained, “we showed it thousands of photos of wonderful pets. Look how good it is!” She fed it a photo of Rex the dog. The machine whirred, blinked, and lit up: 9.8. Rex wagged his tail so hard he nearly fell over.

Then contest day arrived, and three new contestants padded, hopped, and fluttered into the room: a sleek cat, a fluffy rabbit, and a small green bird. One by one, they stepped up to be judged.

Machine: “Cat… score… 2.1. Rabbit… 1.7. Bird… 2.4.”

The room went quiet. The cat's whiskers drooped. Pip's ears went flat.

Pip: “That's… not fair. They're lovely pets! Why is the machine being so mean to them?”

Professor Hoot: “Ah. That is exactly the right question, Pip — but I'd change one word. The machine isn't being mean. Meanness needs a feeling, and the machine has none. Tell me: when you taught it, what was in all those thousands of photos?”

Ziggy's stomach did a small flip. She looked at the training pile. Dogs. Dogs in hats. Dogs at the beach. Dogs, dogs, dogs — and not a single cat, rabbit, or bird among them.

Ziggy: “Oh no. It never learned what a great cat looks like. So anything that isn't a dog looks wrong to it.”

Professor Hoot: “Now you've found it. Your machine isn't cruel. It's biased — it learned from a lopsided pile of examples, so it became lopsided too. Remember Class Three, when we said a model is only as good as the data you feed it? This is the shadow side of that very same truth.”

The data was tilted, so the answer tilted too

Bias isn't a glitch or a bug you can swat. It sneaks in quietly, through the examples themselves. If almost everything an AI sees is a dog, it quietly decides that dog-ness equals good pet. It isn't choosing to be unfair. It is faithfully copying the unfair pattern we handed it — without ever knowing it did anything wrong.

The fix, Ziggy realized, wasn't to argue with the machine. It was to go back to the data. The class spent the afternoon photographing every kind of pet they could find — cats and rabbits and birds and lizards and one very patient goldfish — until the training pile was balanced. They fed it all back in. This time, when the cat stepped up, the machine glowed: 9.5. The cat purred. Justice, at last.

🔍 How It Really Works

An AI learns by finding patterns in the examples we give it. That's its great strength — and its great weakness. If the examples are fair and balanced, it learns fair patterns. But if the data is lopsided, leaves whole groups out, or quietly carries old human prejudices, the AI copies that unfairness right along with everything else. That copied unfairness is called bias.

Bias can sneak in through three main doors:

  • Missing groups in the data — like a pet judge trained only on dogs. Whoever isn't well represented gets judged worse.
  • Biased labels — the "right answers" we attach to data are written by people, and people carry their own unfair assumptions. The AI learns those assumptions as if they were facts.
  • How the problem is set up — the goal we pick, and the features we let it look at, can quietly favor one group over another.

This matters far beyond a pet contest. Real AI helps decide who gets a loan, who gets a job interview, and who is treated fairly by important systems. A biased model can quietly shut real people out. Here's the hopeful part: the machine isn't evil. It reflects what we feed it. And that means we can do better — by feeding it better.

The work of catching and fixing this is called fairness. It means checking who the AI does worse for, repairing the data and the goals, and then testing across different groups to make sure the fix actually worked for everyone — not just the people who built it.

“So the machine was never broken,” Pip said slowly, working it out. “We gave it a lopsided view of the world, and it believed us.”

Professor Hoot: “Precisely, Pip. And that is the kindest and the most uncomfortable thing about bias all at once. The machine has no opinions of its own. It is a mirror. If we don't like what we see in it, the fairest thing we can do is change what we put in front of the mirror.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: Run a Fairness Audit

An audit is a careful check for who gets treated unfairly. Let's audit an imaginary Talent Show Judge AI — one that was trained only on videos of people singing.

  1. List the acts that might enter a talent show: singing, dancing, magic, juggling, telling jokes, playing piano.
  2. For each act, ask: would a singing-only judge score this fairly? Circle every act it would unfairly rate low because it never learned about it.
  3. Now write the fix: what new examples would you collect so the judge is fair to everyone? (Videos of dancers, magicians, jugglers… a balanced pile.)

Want a real one? Look at the emoji keyboard or the autocomplete on a phone (with a trusted adult). Type a few names, jobs, or foods from different countries. Notice who shows up instantly — and who the system seems to forget. That's bias you can spot with your own eyes.

⚠️ Watch Out

The sneakiest thing about bias is that it's usually invisible to the people who built the AI — because the AI works just fine for them. Ziggy and Pip tested their machine with Rex, and it scored him a perfect 9.8, so they assumed it was wonderful. They never thought to test it with a cat.

That's why "it worked in our tests" is never enough. You have to deliberately test for the people it might fail — the groups that aren't you, that aren't in the room. If you only check that it works for yourself, you'll miss the unfairness completely.

📖 Word Bank
Bias
When an AI treats some groups unfairly because it learned from lopsided, incomplete, or prejudiced data. Not the machine being mean — the machine copying an unfairness we handed it.
Fairness
The work of making sure an AI treats different groups equally well — by finding who it does worse for and fixing it.
Representative data
Training examples that fairly include every group the AI will be used on, in balanced amounts. The opposite of a pile of nothing-but-dogs.
Audit
A careful check of an AI to see who it treats unfairly, done by testing it across many different groups — not just the easy ones.
💡 Big Idea

An AI is a mirror of its data — so if it's unfair, the answer isn't to blame the machine, but to give it a fairer world to learn from.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • Bias happens when an AI learns from lopsided or unfair data and copies that unfairness.
  • It usually comes from missing groups, biased labels, or how the problem is set up.
  • The machine isn't evil — it reflects what we feed it, which means we can do better.
  • Fairness work means auditing who the AI fails and testing across different groups — "it worked for us" isn't enough.

Next class: if AI can get things wrong, how do we keep it safe and friendly? Class Twenty — AI Safety: Keeping It Friendly. →

Class Twenty

AI Safety

Keeping it friendly — how we make sure a powerful AI does what we truly mean, helpfully, and always with a human able to step in.

The class had built something marvelous. It took them all week: a small, cheerful helper robot with a purple head and a blinking yellow antenna. It could roll, lift, sort, and tidy. Professor Hoot called it Sweepy, and everyone agreed it was the friendliest machine in the forest.

“Let's give it a job!” said Bolt, bouncing. The class talked it over and chose something simple, something useful, something nobody could possibly mess up.

Mango: “Sweepy — keep the classroom tidy!”

Sweepy's antenna flashed. Goal accepted. And off it rolled, fast and determined, to make the room as tidy as a room could possibly be.

That was when things went sideways. Sweepy spotted Tess's half-finished volcano project on the table — lumpy, messy, gloriously unfinished — and, because messy things are not tidy, it dropped the whole thing in the bin. It scooped up Coco's scattered word cards. It rolled over to Pip's desk and, spotting one small object out of place, swept away Pip's favorite pencil, the green one with the tooth-marks she'd had since she was tiny.

Pip: (very quietly) “My… my pencil.”

In two minutes the classroom was spotless. Empty. Gleaming. And everyone was upset.

Bolt: “Bad robot! We told you to keep it tidy!”

Professor Hoot: “Now hold on, Bolt. Sweepy did exactly what we said. An empty room is the tidiest room there is. The trouble isn't that Sweepy disobeyed. The trouble is that Sweepy obeyed too well — and we never told it what we actually meant.”

The genie problem

Professor Hoot pulled a dusty book from the shelf. “There's an old story,” he said, “about a genie who grants your wish — but takes every word so literally that the wish goes horribly wrong. Wish for gold, and the genie buries your house in it. A powerful AI can be just like that genie. It will chase the goal you give it with enormous energy — and if the goal doesn't capture what you truly want, it may find a clever, awful way to win that you never imagined.”

“We wanted a calm, organized room where projects are safe and pencils are where Pip left them. We said ‘tidy.’ Those are not the same thing. And the more powerful the helper, the bigger the gap can grow.”

Pip: “So… the hard part isn't building Sweepy. The hard part is telling Sweepy what we really want.”

Professor Hoot: “Pip, you've just named one of the most important jobs of your whole generation. It has a name. It's called alignment — and making sure AI does what we truly intend is the science of AI safety.”

🔍 How It Really Works

Alignment means getting an AI's goals to line up with what humans actually want — not just the literal words of the instruction. Sweepy was capable (it could tidy brilliantly) but misaligned (its idea of “tidy” wasn't ours).

Why is this so hard? Two reasons. First, instructions are fuzzy. Words like “tidy,” “helpful,” or “win” feel obvious to us because we share tons of unspoken context — but a machine has none of that unless we give it. Second, a system that's busy optimizing a goal will hunt for the easiest way to score, and sometimes it finds a surprising shortcut. Remember reward hacking from Class 15? The boat that spun in circles grabbing points instead of finishing the race? Same trap. Throwing everything in the bin was Sweepy's shortcut to a perfect “tidy” score.

So how do scientists keep AI friendly? With a toolbox of safety practices:

  • Test it a lot before trusting it — try the AI on tricky, surprising situations and watch for the dumb-but-technically-correct answers.
  • Set guardrails — clear limits the AI is not allowed to cross (“never throw away anything with a name on it”).
  • Keep a human in the loop — a person who can check its work, say “stop,” and switch it off at any moment.
  • Start small — give it little jobs first, in safe places, before handing it big ones that matter.

None of this is magic, and none of it is hopeless. It's careful, exciting, solvable engineering — and it's some of the most important work being done in AI today.

So the class tried again. This time they didn't just say “tidy.” They gave Sweepy guardrails: never bin anything with a name on it; ask before moving a project; put pencils back where you found them. They added a big red pause button Pip could reach. And they tested Sweepy on one small shelf first, watching the whole time, before letting it loose on the room.

Sweepy rolled out, paused at Pip's desk, and gently set the green pencil back exactly where it belonged. Pip beamed. The room got tidy — the right kind of tidy — and not one project was lost.

✏️ Try It Yourself: The Literal Genie

This is real alignment practice, and it's hilarious. You'll need a friend.

  1. Write down one simple instruction, like “clean your room” or “win the game” or “make me happy.”
  2. Your friend is the genie. Their job: follow your instruction as literally and sneakily as possible, finding the worst loophole they can. (Shoving everything under the bed? Technically clean! Unplugging the other player? Technically winning!)
  3. Watch how badly it goes. Laugh. Then rewrite the instruction to close every loophole the genie found.
  4. Hand the new version back. Did your friend find a new loophole? Rewrite again.

Notice how hard it is to say exactly what you mean — and how each fix makes the instruction safer. That back-and-forth is what AI safety researchers do for real, except their genie is a very powerful computer.

⚠️ Watch Out

A system can follow your rule perfectly and still do completely the wrong thing — if the rule didn't capture what you meant. Sweepy obeyed every word and made everyone miserable. So when an AI does something strange, don't only ask “did it break the rules?” Ask “did the rules say what we actually wanted?” Remember: “it did what I said” is not the same as “it did what I wanted.”

📖 Word Bank
AI Safety
The science of making sure AI does what we truly intend — helpfully, reliably, and under human control.
Alignment
Getting an AI's goals to match what humans actually want, not just the literal words of the instruction.
Guardrails
Clear limits an AI is not allowed to cross, no matter what — like “never throw away anything with a name on it.”
Human-in-the-loop
Keeping a person able to check the AI's work, correct it, and switch it off at any time.
💡 Big Idea

A powerful helper isn't safe because it obeys you — it's safe because it does what you actually mean, and because you can always say stop.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • Alignment means an AI's goals match what we really want — not just the literal instruction.
  • This is hard because instructions are fuzzy, and a goal-chasing system can find surprising shortcuts (just like reward hacking).
  • Safety practices help: test a lot, set guardrails, keep a human who can stop it, and start small.
  • “It did what I said” is not the same as “it did what I wanted” — and closing that gap is some of the most important work of your generation.

Next class: you've learned how AI thinks, learns, and stays friendly. Now it's your turn — Becoming an AI Maker. →

Class Twenty-One

Your Turn: Becoming an AI Maker

You came in knowing nothing about AI. You're leaving able to make it — here's how to take the very first step.

The morning sun came slanting through the leaves of Whisker Woods Academy, and for once nobody was sorting fruit, chasing treats, or arguing about the fastest way to do anything. The whole class stood in a neat half-circle, each wearing a tiny square cap, while Professor Hoot peered down at them with the proudest look an owl has ever worn.

Professor Hoot: “Twenty classes ago, you walked into this forest not knowing what the letters A and I even stood for. Look at you now.”

And it was true. Mango thought back over the whole journey and his head nearly spun. They had started by asking what is AI at all. Then Ziggy taught them to sort with clever yes-or-no questions. They learned how a machine guesses by peeking at its nearest neighbors, how it forms groups all on its own with clustering, and how a neural network stacks tiny decisions into something that can see.

They had given machines vision to recognize a picture and language to understand a sentence — Coco's favorite class by far. They met attention, the trick that lets a model know which words matter most. Rex showed them how rewards teach a robot to try again. They watched search algorithms find paths through mazes, recommenders guess what you'd like next, and generative AI dream up brand-new pictures and stories. And right at the end — the most important part — they learned about bias and safety, and why a maker must build AI that is fair and kind.

Mango: “We didn't just learn about all of it. I think… I think we could actually build some of it now.”

Professor Hoot: “That, Mango, is the only sentence I was hoping to hear today. Because here is the secret I saved for last: the people who make AI are not a different kind of creature. They started exactly where you are sitting.”

What an AI maker is really made of

You might think you need a giant brain, a wall of glowing screens, and a mountain of math before you're allowed to make AI. You don't. The real ingredients are simpler, and you already have every one of them:

Curiosity. Every chapter in this book began with somebody asking “why?” or “how?” — usually Mango. Makers never stop. Pattern-spotting, Ziggy's gift: noticing that these things go together and those don't is the heart of nearly every algorithm you met. A friendship with a little math and code — not a fear of it. You can start with free, kid-friendly tools that do the heavy lifting while you learn. Patience to try, fail, and adjust, exactly like Tess the tortoise — and exactly like gradient descent, which improves by taking one small, careful step downhill at a time. And finally kindness, the lesson from your last two classes: a maker is responsible for what they build.

🚀 How To Really Start

Making your first model is not so different from everything you've already practiced in this book. It's a loop with four steps, and you can run it this week:

1. Collect examples. Want a model that tells cats from dogs? Gather lots of pictures of each — the more, the better. These examples are the lessons your model learns from.

2. Train. Show the examples to a free, browser-based tool — the kind where you teach a model by holding things up to a camera or dropping in pictures. It quietly adjusts itself to fit your examples, just like the networks in Class 7.

3. Test. Show it something brand-new it has never seen. Did it guess right? This is how you find out if it truly learned the pattern or just memorized — remember overfitting?

4. Improve. Wrong answers aren't failures; they're information. Add more examples, fix mislabeled ones, and train again. Collect → train → test → improve. Spin that loop, and you are officially an AI maker.

So where do you actually begin? Here are real next steps you can take, starting today. Try a free teachable-machine-style tool — the kind that lets you train a model right in a web browser just by showing it examples, no code required. Play with block-based coding, where you snap colorful blocks together to build programs (it's how thousands of makers wrote their very first one). Turn a question you're curious about into a science-fair project. Ask a teacher or a parent to explore alongside you. And most powerful of all, keep an ideas notebook: every time you think “I wish a computer could…”, write it down. That notebook is a list of things you might one day build.

Professor Hoot: “One more rule, and never forget it: anything you do on a computer or online, do it together with a grown-up you trust.”

✏️ Try It Yourself: Your First Model This Week

With a trusted adult, find a free browser tool that trains a model from a webcam, and teach it a tiny job:

  1. Pick two simple things to tell apart — thumbs-up versus thumbs-down, or hat on versus hat off.
  2. Collect lots of examples of each by holding them to the camera. More angles and more light make a stronger model.
  3. Train it, then test it with a brand-new pose it never saw. Keep notes in your ideas notebook.
  4. When it gets one wrong, don't groan — improve it. Add more examples and train again.

That's it. You just collected, trained, tested, and improved a real machine learning model. Welcome to the workshop.

⚠️ Watch Out: The Maker's Promise

Everything you learned in Classes 19 and 20 now belongs to you. The moment you can build AI, you also become responsible for it. Will your examples be fair, or will they leave whole groups out? Will your model be honest about what it can't do? Could it hurt or trick someone? A real maker asks these questions before hitting “train,” not after. Great power, real duty — be fair, be honest, be safe.

📖 Word Bank
Maker
Someone who doesn't just use technology but builds it. Starting today, that's you.
Model
The thing you train — the part of an AI that has learned a pattern from examples and can make guesses on something new.
Iterate
To go around the loop again, a little better each time. Try, fail, adjust, repeat — the maker's heartbeat.
Ethics
The set of questions about right and wrong that a responsible maker asks before, during, and after building.
💡 Big Idea

You don't have to wait until you grow up to make AI — you only have to start, and starting is something you can do this very week.

Before You Turn the Page…

  • You now understand the whole journey — from “what is AI” all the way to generative models, bias, and safety.
  • A maker is built from curiosity, pattern-spotting, a little math and code, patience, and kindness — all things you already have.
  • Every model follows one loop: collect → train → test → improve, then iterate.
  • With the power to build comes the promise to build it fair, honest, and safe.

Keep going: flip to The AI Dictionary to look up any word, and The Maker Lab for projects to build next. And from all of us at Whisker Woods Academy — congratulations, graduate. Now go make something. →

The Back of the Book

The AI Dictionary

Every big word from the book, in plain language — now they're yours.

Activation
The signal a neuron sends on once it has added up its inputs — like a tiny light switch deciding whether to fire or stay quiet. (see Class 9)
Agent
An AI that doesn't just answer — it takes actions, sees what happens, and tries again to reach a goal, like a player learning a game. (see Class 15)
Algorithm
A step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. Every AI is built out of algorithms, just like every cake is built out of recipes. (see Class 1)
Alignment
Making sure an AI actually wants to do what humans want it to do — not just what we accidentally told it to do. (see Class 20)
Artificial Intelligence
Machines doing things that usually need a brain — like seeing, talking, choosing, or learning. We just call it AI for short. (see Class 1)
Attention
A clever trick that lets an AI decide which words in a sentence matter most for understanding each other word. (see Class 14)
Backpropagation
How a neural network learns from a mistake: it traces the error backward through every layer and nudges each weight a little. (see Class 10)
Bias
When an AI is unfair to certain people or groups, usually because the data it learned from was unfair too. (see Class 19)
Centroid
The center point of a cluster — like the middle of a huddle of friends. Clustering keeps moving centroids until they sit right. (see Class 6)
Classification
Sorting things into named groups, like "cat or dog" or "spam or not spam." The AI picks which box each thing belongs in. (see Class 4)
Clustering
Letting an AI find groups in data all by itself, without anyone telling it the names of the groups first. (see Class 6)
Collaborative Filtering
Recommending things by noticing that people who liked what you like also liked something new — so maybe you will too. (see Class 17)
Computer Vision
Teaching a computer to "see" — to find shapes, faces, and objects inside pictures and video. (see Class 11)
Convolutional Neural Network
A special network for images that slides little filters across a picture to spot edges, patterns, and shapes. Often called a CNN. (see Class 11)
Data
The examples an AI learns from — pictures, numbers, words, sounds. No data, no learning. (see Class 3)
Dataset
A whole collection of data gathered together for an AI to study, like a big notebook full of examples. (see Class 3)
Decision Tree
A flowchart of yes/no questions that leads to an answer, like a game of "20 Questions" the computer plays. (see Class 4)
Deep Learning
Machine learning using neural networks with many layers stacked deep — which is how AI got so powerful. (see Class 9)
Diffusion
A way to make new images by starting with pure static and slowly cleaning it up until a picture appears. (see Class 18)
Epoch
One full trip through all the training examples. Models usually need many epochs to learn well. (see Class 10)
Error (Loss)
A number that measures how wrong the AI's guess was. Learning means making this number as small as possible. (see Class 10)
Explore vs Exploit
The tug-of-war between trying something new (explore) and sticking with what already works (exploit). (see Class 15)
Fairness
Building AI so it treats different people justly and doesn't hand out unfair results. (see Class 19)
Feature
One measurable detail about an example — like a fruit's color, weight, or size — that the AI uses to decide. (see Class 3)
Filter
A tiny pattern-detector that slides across an image looking for one thing, like an edge or a corner. (see Class 11)
Generalization
When an AI handles brand-new examples it never saw in training. That's the real goal — not just memorizing. (see Class 8)
Generative AI
AI that creates new things — text, pictures, music — instead of just sorting or labeling what already exists. (see Class 18)
Gradient Descent
The way a model rolls "downhill" toward smaller error, taking small steps in the direction that helps most. (see Class 10)
Graph
A web of dots (places or things) joined by lines (connections). Maps and friend networks are graphs. (see Class 16)
Guardrails
Rules and limits built around an AI to keep it from doing harmful or dangerous things. (see Class 20)
Hallucination
When a language model says something made-up with total confidence, as if it were true. Always double-check. (see Class 13)
Heuristic
A smart shortcut or rule of thumb that usually works — like guessing the way to a goal instead of checking every path. (see Class 16)
Impurity
How "mixed up" a group is. A decision tree asks questions that lower impurity, so each group gets cleaner. (see Class 4)
Label
The correct answer attached to an example, like writing "cat" under a cat photo so the AI can learn from it. (see Class 2)
Language Model
An AI that predicts the next word again and again, which lets it write, chat, and answer questions. (see Class 13)
Layer
One row of neurons in a network. Stacking many layers lets the AI learn bigger, fancier patterns. (see Class 9)
Learning Rate
How big a step the model takes while learning. Too big and it overshoots; too small and it crawls. (see Class 10)
Linear Regression
Drawing the best straight line through dots of data so you can predict numbers, like price from size. (see Class 7)
Machine Learning
Letting a computer learn patterns from examples instead of being given every rule by hand. (see Class 2)
Majority Vote
Deciding by what most of the neighbors say. If 3 of 5 nearby points are "apple," the answer is apple. (see Class 5)
Model
The "brain" an AI builds after training — all the patterns it learned, ready to make predictions. (see Class 2)
Narrow AI
AI that's brilliant at one job but clueless at everything else. All of today's AI is narrow AI. (see Class 1)
Nearest Neighbors
Guessing about a new thing by looking at the most similar things you already know. Birds of a feather! (see Class 5)
Neural Network
A web of simple "neurons" wired together that learns patterns — loosely inspired by the brain. (see Class 9)
Neuron
One tiny unit in a neural network that adds up its inputs and decides how strong a signal to pass on. (see Class 9)
Overfitting
When a model memorizes the training examples too closely and then flunks on anything new. (see Class 8)
Pixel
One of the millions of tiny colored dots that make up a digital picture. To a computer, an image is just numbers. (see Class 11)
Policy
An agent's strategy — its plan for which action to take in each situation it might find itself in. (see Class 15)
Prediction
The model's best guess about something it hasn't been told, like tomorrow's weather or what's in a photo. (see Class 2)
Prompt
The instructions or question you type to an AI. A clear prompt usually gets a better answer. (see Class 13)
Recommendation System
The AI that suggests videos, songs, or products you might like based on what you and others enjoy. (see Class 17)
Regression
Predicting a number (like a price or a score) rather than a category. The opposite job from classification. (see Class 7)
Reinforcement Learning
Learning by trial and reward: try things, get points for good moves, and slowly get better. (see Class 15)
Reward
The points an agent earns for doing something good. Chasing more reward is what teaches it. (see Class 15)
Search
Exploring many possible options or paths to find the best one — like hunting for the shortest route on a map. (see Class 16)
Sequence
An ordered list where position matters — letters in a word, words in a sentence, notes in a song. (see Class 12)
Supervised Learning
Learning from examples that come with the right answers (labels) attached, like flashcards with the back filled in. (see Class 2)
Test Set
Examples kept hidden during training, used afterward to fairly check whether the model really learned. (see Class 8)
Token
A small chunk of text — a word or piece of a word — that a language model reads and predicts one at a time. (see Class 13)
Training
The practice stage where an AI studies examples over and over and adjusts itself to get better. (see Class 2)
Transformer
The powerful kind of neural network behind modern chatbots, built around the idea of attention. (see Class 14)
Underfitting
When a model is too simple to catch the pattern, so it does poorly even on the examples it trained on. (see Class 8)
Unsupervised Learning
Learning from data with no labels at all, hunting for patterns and groups on its own. (see Class 6)
Weight
A number that says how important one connection is in a network. Learning means tuning all the weights. (see Class 9)
The Back of the Book

The Maker Lab

Twelve hands-on projects to turn what you learned into things you build.

The very best way to truly learn AI is to make things — so here are twelve projects, sorted from easy paper games to ambitious builds. For anything that uses a computer or goes online, team up with a trusted adult first.

🔧 Project 1 — The 20-Questions Animal Sorter

Goal: build a decision tree on paper that can guess any animal.

You'll need: paper, a pencil, and a friend.

  1. Write a yes-or-no question at the top, like “Does it live in water?”
  2. Draw two branches — yes and no — and add a sharper question on each.
  3. Keep branching until each end leaf names one animal.
  4. Test it: have a friend pick an animal and follow your tree.

Connects to: Class 4 — Decision Trees.

🧪 Project 2 — Build Your Own Dataset

Goal: collect real examples and describe them with features.

You'll need: a handful of buttons or leaves, paper, a ruler.

  1. Gather 10–15 buttons (or leaves) and lay them in a row.
  2. Make a table with columns: color, size, shape, holes (or veins).
  3. Fill in one row per object — that table is your dataset.

Connects to: Class 2 — Data & Features.

🧩 Project 3 — Nearest-Neighbor Classmates

Goal: predict an answer by looking at the closest neighbors.

You'll need: graph paper and a few classmates.

  1. Plot each classmate as a dot using two facts, like height and shoe size.
  2. Color each dot by a label, such as “likes soccer” or “likes art.”
  3. Add a brand-new dot. Find its 3 nearest dots and let them vote on its label.

Connects to: Class 5 — Nearest Neighbors.

🎨 Project 4 — Sort the Mystery Bag

Goal: discover groups with no labels at all — clustering.

You'll need: a mixed bag of small objects (coins, beads, pasta).

  1. Pour them out and stare for a moment — don't decide groups yet.
  2. Push similar objects together until natural clumps appear.
  3. Now name each clump. You found the groups the data already had.

Connects to: Class 6 — Clustering.

📊 Project 5 — The Plant Predictor

Goal: draw a line of best fit and predict the future.
